Both letters are addressed to Kenneth McKellar, concern the Army civil-functions appropriations bill, characterize House reductions to flood-control and river-and-harbor funds as false economy, explain that the President's budget was already constrained by national-security needs, warn that the cuts would stop new projects and interrupt projects underway, invoke recent destructive floods, advocate steady rather than stop-and-go river development, identify several of the same projects, and conclude by urging restoration of the requested funds. C10 shares much of the policy argument and some phrasing, but it is addressed to a labor leader and lacks the same appropriations-letter structure. C07 parallels the appeal to restore House-cut public-works funds but focuses primarily on transmission policy.","shared_material":[{"child_excerpt":"the House reduced my budget requests for flood control and river and harbor development by 29 percent. The effect of this reduction would be to stop construction on a number of projects now underway, to slow down work on many others, and to prevent starting certain new projects","parent_excerpt":"The House cut my budget requests for this important work by nearly 20 per cent... The House action would prevent any of the new projects from being started, would force the suspension of work on some projects now underway, and would seriously delay work on a whole range of projects","explanation":"The later letter closely reuses the earlier description of a House percentage cut and its three operational consequences: preventing starts, stopping existing construction, and delaying other work."},{"child_excerpt":"I appreciate the desire of the Members of the House to hold budget expenditures for civil public works to a minimum at a time when we have to put so much money into national security programs... I firmly believe that to cut below the Budget estimates would lose us far more than would be \"saved.\"","parent_excerpt":"We can spend little enough on this kind of work in emergency times like the present... because of the urgent need for large expenditures for national security... I believe this cut was false economy.","explanation":"Both defend an already austere public-works budget against further cuts by juxtaposing national-security stringency with the false economy of reducing flood-control spending."},{"child_excerpt":"The proper way... is to move forward steadily, year by year, toward the orderly and economic completion of projects now underway... These problems cannot be handled efficiently on an intermittent, stop-and-go basis.","parent_excerpt":"I cannot over-emphasize the importance of steady, well planned progress in this field--as contrasted with hasty, stop-and-go action... The budget requests now before the Congress are part of an orderly program for the development of our great rivers","explanation":"The distinctive contrast between steady, orderly progress and stop-and-go development is substantially repeated."},{"child_excerpt":"The Budget contains funds, for example, for starting Ice Harbor Dam... Tuttle Creek... and... Gavins Point","parent_excerpt":"the present supplemental estimates... will provide for work on the Tuttle Creek... In particular... Gavins Point Dam... and Ice Harbor... on all of which construction should be started immediately.","explanation":"The later letter carries forward several of the same named projects within the same argument for full appropriations."}]}
